sources.title: Introduction to AI and Data Science

questions.q: What does the Turing test evaluate?
o: Whether a program uses human reasoning steps internally
Whether a program solves logic problems correctly
Whether a program behaves indistinguishably from a human
Whether a program improves with more training data
questions.e: The Turing test belongs to acting humanly: only behaviour is observed.

questions.q: Which capability lets a Turing-test program adapt to new circumstances and extrapolate patterns?
questions.e: The slide assigns adapting and detecting patterns to machine learning.

questions.q: The syllogism "Socrates is a man; all men are mortal" is the classic example of which approach?
questions.e: Laws of thought and syllogisms define thinking rationally, which initiated logic.

questions.q: A reflex that pulls your hand from a hot surface illustrates which point?
o: Human reflexes cannot be modeled by any agent
Rationality requires explicit laws of thought
Rational agents must always reason logically first
Behaviour can be rational without careful deliberation
questions.e: The slide uses it to show that logical thinking is only one part of appropriate behaviour.

questions.q: Which statement about AI and machine learning is correct?
o: Machine learning is AI, but not all AI is machine learning
AI is one branch inside the field of machine learning
AI and machine learning are two names for one field
All AI systems learn patterns from historical data
questions.e: AI is the umbrella; ML is one of its branches.

questions.q: How does machine learning differ from traditional programming?
o: It takes rules and answers and produces the data
It takes data and rules and produces the answers
It takes data and answers and produces the rules
It needs neither historical data nor expected answers
questions.e: Data plus rules giving answers describes traditional programming.

questions.q: A set of JSON records from a web API is best classified as:
questions.e: JSON has keys and nesting without a fixed tabular schema.

questions.q: A sensor feed that delivers thousands of readings every second mainly illustrates which Big Data challenge?
questions.e: Velocity is the speed at which data is generated.

questions.q: A dataset contains conflicting and unreliable records. Which V is the concern?
questions.e: Veracity is uncertainty about data quality.

questions.q: In the slide's process, what comes immediately after data cleaning?
questions.e: The order is collection, cleaning, exploration, feature engineering, building, evaluation, deployment.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of exploratory data analysis?
o: To understand data characteristics before modeling
To deploy a trained model into production
To replace data cleaning with visual checks
To compute the final accuracy of a model
questions.e: The slide states EDA's purpose directly.

questions.q: A retailer forecasts next quarter's demand using past sales. This is:
questions.e: It estimates what will happen. Recommending an order size would be prescriptive.

questions.q: A ride-hailing app picks which driver to send to each customer. This is:
questions.e: It recommends the action to take.

questions.q: Name the four approaches to AI and give the defining idea of each.
questions.m: Acting humanly (behave like a person; the Turing test). Thinking humanly (model how people think). Thinking rationally (correct reasoning; logic). Acting rationally (achieve the best outcome).

questions.q: List the seven steps of the data science process in order.
questions.m: Data collection, data cleaning, data exploration, feature engineering, model building, model evaluation, deployment and monitoring.

questions.q: Explain the difference between descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics with one example each.
questions.m: Descriptive says what happened (last month's sales report). Predictive says what will happen (a demand forecast). Prescriptive says what to do next (which driver to dispatch).

questions.q: Which description matches a Pandas Series?
o: A list of DataFrames stored by key
A connection to a SQL table
questions.e: A DataFrame is the two-dimensional table; each of its columns is a Series.

questions.q: What is the index of pd.Series({"a": 10, "b": 20})?
o: No index until one is assigned
questions.e: Dictionary keys become the index.

questions.q: How many values does pd.Series(5, index=[0, 1, 2, 3]) contain?
questions.e: A scalar is repeated once for every index label.

questions.q: For a Series with default index, what does s[1:4] return?
o: Only the elements at positions 1 and 4
questions.e: Position slices exclude the end.

questions.q: For labels a to e, what does s["a":"c"] return?
o: Only the elements labeled a and c
The elements labeled b and c
The elements labeled a, b and c
The elements labeled a and b
questions.e: Label slices include the end label.

questions.q: What does df[["Name", "Age"]] return?
o: The first two rows of the table
A DataFrame with those two columns
questions.e: A list of columns returns a DataFrame.

questions.q: Which filter is written correctly?
questions.e: Use & with parentheses around each condition.

questions.q: What does df.iloc[:3, 1:3] select?
o: Rows labeled 3 and columns labeled 1 to 3
questions.e: iloc uses integer positions with exclusive ends.

questions.q: Which read_csv parameter loads only certain columns?
questions.e: usecols selects columns to read.

questions.q: What does pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=None) return?
o: Only the first sheet as a DataFrame
Only the last sheet as a DataFrame
A dictionary of DataFrames, one per sheet
questions.e: The slide says None reads all sheets into a dictionary.

questions.q: JSON shaped as a list of row dictionaries matches which orient?
questions.e: records means a list of dictionaries, one per row.

questions.q: Which if_exists value adds new rows to an existing SQL table?
questions.e: replace drops the table, and fail raises an error.

questions.q: Which call writes newline-delimited JSON?
questions.e: lines=True is only valid with orient="records".

questions.q: Explain the difference between loc and iloc, including how each treats the end of a slice.
questions.m: loc selects by label or condition and its slice end is inclusive. iloc selects by integer position and its slice end is exclusive.

questions.q: Write code that selects the Name and Age columns, then explain why two pairs of brackets are needed.
questions.m: df[["Name", "Age"]]. The inner brackets are a Python list of column names; the outer ones index the DataFrame, and the result is a DataFrame.

questions.q: Describe the three if_exists options in to_sql.
questions.m: replace drops the table and recreates it, append inserts into the existing table, and fail raises an error if the table already exists.

questions.q: In the nutrition data, "situation" (living alone, as a couple, with family) is best described as:
o: A design variable that defines a group
An identifier column for each row
A measurement that varies per person
questions.e: It describes which group a person belongs to, not a measured outcome.

questions.q: Why is header=None passed when reading abalone.data?
o: The file has no row of column names
The file is not comma separated
It removes the first row of data
It makes column names come from row 2
questions.e: Without it, Pandas treats the first data row as headers.

questions.q: The number of births in a hospital per day is:
questions.e: A count has a countable set of possible values.

questions.q: Eye color with values blue, black, brown and green is:
questions.e: It has a fixed set of categories with no numeric meaning.

questions.q: Why did Python treat all 13 nutri features as quantitative at first?
o: read_excel always converts text to integers
The file had no column names to read
They were entered as whole numbers
questions.e: Category codes were stored as integers.

questions.q: Which line correctly recodes gender?
questions.e: replace maps codes to labels; astype sets the type.

questions.q: What does describe report for a categorical column?
questions.e: The numeric summary applies only to quantitative features.

questions.q: What does margins=True add to pd.crosstab?
questions.e: It adds the All row and column.

questions.q: The 0.75 sample quantile is also called:
questions.e: 25, 50 and 75 percentiles are the first, second and third quartiles.

questions.q: If the sample variance is 81, what is the standard deviation?
questions.e: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

questions.q: Which plot should show how height relates to weight?
questions.e: Two quantitative variables.

questions.q: To compare coffee consumption between men and women, use:
questions.e: One qualitative and one quantitative variable.

questions.q: Explain the difference between design variables and measurement variables with an example of each.
questions.m: Design variables are fixed before collection and describe conditions or groups, such as gender, and act as predictors. Measurement variables record what was observed, such as height, and are what we explain or predict.

questions.q: Define the p-sample quantile.
questions.m: A value x such that at least a fraction p of the data is less than or equal to x and at least a fraction 1-p is greater than or equal to x.

questions.q: In the crosstab, 78 of 141 women and 20 of 85 men are single. State the conclusion and why you use proportions.
questions.m: About 55% of women and 24% of men are single, so the proportion of single men is smaller. Proportions are needed because the group sizes differ.

questions.q: Which expression gives the number of missing values per column?
questions.e: True counts as 1, so sum counts the missing entries.

questions.q: Students who registered late have no Major 1 score because they had not yet taken it. This is:
questions.e: The missingness depends on other observed data, the registration date.

questions.q: A student who failed the final deliberately skips submitting it. This is:
questions.e: The chance of missing depends on the missing value itself.

questions.q: A project column is skewed by a few zero scores. Which fill is most defensible?
questions.e: The median is less affected by outliers.

questions.q: Forward fill is best suited to:
questions.e: It uses the neighbouring value, which needs a meaningful order.

questions.q: What does df.dropna(axis=1) do?
o: Removes only rows that are entirely empty
Fills missing values with column means
questions.e: axis=1 refers to columns.

questions.q: What does thresh control in dropna?
o: The value used to fill missing cells
The maximum number of rows to remove
The percentage of rows to fill
The minimum number of non-null values to keep
questions.e: Rows or columns below the threshold are dropped.

questions.q: Define MCAR, MAR and MNAR.
questions.m: MCAR: unrelated to any value. MAR: depends on other observed data. MNAR: depends on the missing value itself.

questions.q: Why should you not fill every column with its mean?
questions.m: The mean is sensitive to outliers and skew, and filling MNAR data can bias results and hide important cases. The right approach depends on what the column means.

questions.q: In Y = f(X) + error, what does the error term capture?
o: The difference between training and test loss
The slope of the fitted regression line
The features left out of the training set
questions.e: The slide defines it that way.

questions.q: Predicting whether a tumour is benign or malignant is:
questions.e: The response lies in a finite set of classes.

questions.q: What is the zero-one loss when the predicted class equals the true class?
questions.e: It incurs 1 only when they differ.

questions.q: Risk is best defined as:
o: The expected loss over the data distribution
The squared distance of one prediction
The average loss on the training set
The loss on a single observation
questions.e: Risk is E Loss(Y, g(X)).

questions.q: The regression function at X = x is:
questions.e: It is the conditional average, and it minimizes mean squared error.

questions.q: Why does prediction error remain even if we knew f exactly?
o: At each x there is a distribution of possible Y values
The training set can never be large enough
The model class is always too simple
questions.e: That spread is the irreducible error.

questions.q: Which method is unsupervised on the slides?
questions.e: PCA learns structure with no response variable.

questions.q: Which term is an expectation over the true distribution?
questions.e: Training loss is a sample average; loss and error apply to one point.

questions.q: The learner is defined as the function in class G that:
o: Fits only the test sample exactly
questions.e: True risk is unavailable, so training loss is minimized.

questions.q: A model has zero training loss but poor predictions on new data. This is:
questions.e: Poor generalization despite minimal training loss.

questions.q: What makes test loss an unbiased estimate of generalization risk?
o: The test sample is larger than training
The test loss is always lower
The test sample is separate from training
The test sample uses a different distribution
questions.e: It must be independent of the training data.

questions.q: If the test set is used for model selection, what else is needed?
o: A third set for final testing
questions.e: The slide calls for a third set once selection uses the second.

questions.q: Distinguish error, loss, training loss and risk.
questions.m: Error is a general distance between a true value and its approximation. Loss is a specific function for one prediction. Training or test loss is the sample average of the loss. Risk is the expected loss over the true distribution.

questions.q: State the reducible and irreducible parts of expected squared error and how each can be changed.
questions.m: The reducible part is the squared gap between the estimate and f; a better model lowers it. The irreducible part is Var(error), which comes from randomness and no model can remove.

questions.q: Explain why minimizing training loss is not the ultimate goal.
questions.m: A function can match every training pair and reach zero loss but predict new data poorly. The goal is low generalization risk on unseen data.

questions.q: What simplifies the search in a convex optimization problem?
o: The feasible set can be any non-convex shape
The function has several saddle points
Every local minimum is also a global minimum
The gradient is zero at every point
questions.e: That is the defining benefit of convex problems.

questions.q: Why is least-squares linear regression convex?
o: It uses a sigmoid activation function
Its loss is computed on test data
It always has a Hessian of zero
Its objective is quadratic in the parameters
questions.e: A quadratic objective ensures a single global minimum.

questions.q: In which direction does the gradient point?
questions.e: Descent moves opposite to it.

questions.q: The Hessian matrix contains:
questions.e: It describes local curvature.

questions.q: For f(x) = x² - 4x + 4 with the constraint x <= 1, where is the minimum?
questions.e: The unconstrained minimum at 2 is infeasible, and f decreases up to x = 1.

questions.q: Which statement matches the slide comparison?
o: Gradient descent needs the inverse Hessian
questions.e: Gradient descent needs only the gradient.

questions.q: Why does Newton's method struggle on very large problems?
o: Computing and inverting the Hessian becomes infeasible
It only works when the loss is non-convex
It has too many learning rates to tune
It cannot use gradient information at all
questions.e: That cost grows quickly with the number of variables.

questions.q: In x_new = x_old - alpha grad f(x_old), alpha is the:
questions.e: It controls the step size.

questions.q: If MSE is 25, what is the RMSE?
questions.e: RMSE is the square root of MSE.

questions.q: High training error and high test error indicate:
questions.e: The model is too simple to capture the pattern.

questions.q: High variance means the model is:
o: Too sensitive to the training set
questions.e: High variance means it captures random noise.

questions.q: Train error 1%, test error 11%. The diagnosis is:
questions.e: Low train error with a large gap to test error.

questions.q: Compare gradient descent and Newton's method on derivatives, cost per iteration and behaviour on non-convex problems.
questions.m: Gradient descent uses first derivatives, is cheap per iteration and works on non-convex problems, possibly stopping at a local minimum. Newton uses the Hessian, is expensive per iteration and is fast near the minimum, but on non-convex problems it can reach saddle points or diverge.

questions.q: Explain why the update x - eta grad f(x) decreases f.
questions.m: By a first-order Taylor expansion, f changes by about -eta times the squared gradient norm. That norm is non-negative, so f decreases for a small enough eta.

questions.q: Define bias and variance, and say which causes underfitting and which causes overfitting.
questions.m: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions and causes underfitting. Variance is error from sensitivity to the training set and causes overfitting.

questions.q: P(Y=0|x) = 0.10, P(Y=1|x) = 0.70, P(Y=2|x) = 0.20. The optimal classifier under zero-one loss returns:
o: No class, because there is no certainty
questions.e: It picks the class with the highest conditional probability.

questions.q: Why can even the optimal classifier not reach zero error?
o: Its training set is always too small
questions.e: That remaining error is the Bayes error rate.

questions.q: In the dog, cat and possum matrix, what is the misclassification error?
questions.e: Error is 1 - 93/135.

questions.q: For class Dog in the matrix, what is fp?
questions.e: Column sum without the diagonal: 8 + 7.

questions.q: Where do false negatives for class j appear?
o: In column j, off the diagonal
In row j, off the diagonal
Outside row j and column j
questions.e: Actual j predicted as something else.

questions.q: For class Cat, recall is:
questions.e: Recall = tp/(tp + fn) = 22/(22 + 23).

questions.q: For class Cat, precision is:
questions.e: Precision = tp/(tp + fp) = 22/(22 + 6).

questions.q: What does specificity measure?
o: Of all real j objects, how many were found
The share of all predictions that are correct
Of all non-j objects, how many were rejected
Of everything called j, how many are j
questions.e: Specificity = tn/(fp + tn).

questions.q: Which classifier suits the secure facility, and why?
o: Classifier 2, since it admits more people
Classifier 1, since its accuracy is far higher
Classifier 1, since false positives are costly
Classifier 2, since its recall is higher
questions.e: The accuracies are nearly equal; precision decides.

questions.q: A spam filter must never send real email to junk. Which metric matters most for the spam class?
o: Specificity of the non-spam class only
questions.e: A false positive sends real email to junk.

questions.q: True labels {a, b}, predicted {b, c}. What are precision and recall?
questions.e: One correct of two predicted and of two actual.

questions.q: For true {a, b} and predicted {b, c}, multilabel accuracy is:
questions.e: Intersection 1 over union 3.

questions.q: Exact match ratio counts an object as correct only when:
o: More than half of the labels are right
At least one predicted label is right
The whole predicted set equals the true set
The predicted set is inside the true set
questions.e: It is the strict metric.

questions.q: Explain the Bayes error rate.
questions.m: It is the smallest possible expected loss under zero-one loss, P(Y != g*(X)). It is irreducible because classes overlap, so even the optimal classifier makes mistakes.

questions.q: A confusion matrix has rows Dog [30, 2, 6], Cat [8, 22, 15], Possum [7, 4, 41]. For Possum, find tp, fp, fn and tn.
Why can accuracy be misleading? Use an example.
questions.m: With imbalanced classes or unequal error costs, accuracy can stay high while important mistakes happen. A 99.55% accurate facility guard still admitted 50 intruders, which precision reveals.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of label encoding on a nominal feature?
o: It introduces an order that may not exist
It always creates too many columns
questions.e: The slide states this directly.

questions.q: A feature has three categories. One-hot encoding as on the slide produces:
questions.e: One binary column per category.

questions.q: What does the logistic function do?
o: Sums the feature values to one
Rounds scores to the nearest integer
Maps probabilities to the whole real line
questions.e: The logit does the reverse mapping.

questions.q: The logit of p is:
questions.e: It is the log-odds.

questions.q: At p = 0.5, what is the logit?
Why is the log-likelihood used?
o: It removes the need for training data
It turns the model into a linear regression
It changes which parameters are best
It turns products of probabilities into sums
questions.e: It simplifies computation and improves stability.

questions.q: Why are both num and Target dropped from X?
o: Pandas cannot process those two columns
Target comes from num, so num would leak the answer
questions.e: Keeping num would reveal the label.

questions.q: What does model.score(X_test, y_test) return for logistic regression?
questions.e: The slide notes the variable name is misleading.

questions.q: In a classification report, support means:
o: The number of actual occurrences of each class
The number of predictions per class
questions.e: It counts actual occurrences.

questions.q: Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 usually does what?
questions.e: More cases are called positive.

questions.q: The x-axis of an ROC curve is:
questions.e: FPR is 1 - specificity.

questions.q: What does the ROC diagonal represent?
questions.e: It has no discrimination ability.

questions.q: An AUC of 0.5 means:
questions.e: 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is random.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between the logit and the sigmoid.
questions.m: They are inverses. The logit maps a probability to log-odds, which equal the linear combination of features. The sigmoid maps the linear score back to a probability between 0 and 1.

questions.q: Why do precision and recall alone not fully evaluate a classifier?
questions.m: They depend on one decision threshold, say nothing about other thresholds, and can mislead on imbalanced data. ROC and AUC evaluate across thresholds.

questions.q: In a heart disease model, which metric would you prioritize and why?
questions.m: Recall for the disease class, because a false negative is a missed patient, which is the most serious error in this setting.

questions.q: After standardization, a feature has:
questions.e: z = (x - mean) / std.

questions.q: Which scaling maps values into [0, 1]?
questions.e: x' = (x - min) / (max - min).

questions.q: How does unscaled data affect gradient descent?
o: It zigzags and needs a tiny learning rate
It always reaches a saddle point
It no longer requires a gradient
It converges in exactly one step
questions.e: The loss surface becomes a long, narrow valley.

questions.q: What is wrong with scaling the whole dataset before splitting?
o: Scaling only works on one column
The features lose their column names
The model can no longer use the test set
questions.e: Test rows influence the mean and standard deviation.

questions.q: Which scaler is least sensitive to outliers?
questions.e: It uses the median and IQR.

questions.q: What automatically applies the fit-on-training rule in cross-validation?
o: The fit_transform call on all data
questions.e: The slide names Pipeline.

questions.q: Describe the correct order of scaling and modeling, and the risk of doing it wrongly.
questions.m: Split first. Fit the scaler on training data, transform the training and test sets with those statistics, then fit the model. Scaling everything first leaks test information and makes the score too optimistic.

questions.q: A salary column has one extreme outlier. Which scaler do you choose and why?
questions.m: RobustScaler, because the median and IQR are barely affected by a single outlier, whereas min-max would squeeze the other values into a tiny range.

questions.q: What does an embedding model produce?
o: A single probability for each object
A database row for each pixel
A sorted list of class labels
questions.e: Objects become vectors so that similarity can be computed.

questions.q: Why was NumPy far faster than a list in the slide test?
o: Its internals are optimized and C-based
Lists cannot store more than 1,000 items
It skips some elements when summing
It stores data in a Python dictionary
questions.e: The slide gives C-based processing as the reason.
Element-by-element subtraction.

questions.q: What is the dot product of [2, 3, 4] and [1, 0, -1]?
A dot product of 0 between non-zero vectors means they are:
questions.e: Zero means no alignment.

questions.q: What is the L2-normalized form of [3, 4]?
questions.e: Divide by the norm, 5.

questions.q: The L1 norm of [3, -2] is:
questions.e: The sum of absolute values.

questions.q: The L2 norm measures:
questions.e: Euclidean length.

questions.q: What is the cosine similarity of [3, 4] and [4, 3]?
Cosine similarity depends on:
o: How many elements each vector has
The sum of all vector elements
questions.e: Magnitude is divided out.

questions.q: Why can np.dot give cosine similarity after L2 normalization?
o: np.dot divides by the norms itself
Both norms equal 1, so the denominator is 1
questions.e: Dividing by 1 leaves the dot product.

questions.q: Why is cosine similarity often preferred over the raw dot product for comparing text or word embeddings?
questions.m: The raw dot product grows with vector length, so large vectors look similar to everything. Cosine similarity divides out magnitude and compares the angle or direction.

questions.q: Normalize [6, 8] with L2 and state its L1 norm before normalization.
questions.m: The L2 norm is 10, so the normalized vector is [0.6, 0.8]. The L1 norm is 6 + 8 = 14.

questions.q: Why is data standardized before PCA?
o: So the covariance matrix becomes zero
So the eigenvalues all equal one
questions.e: Otherwise large-scale features dominate.

questions.q: The diagonal of a covariance matrix holds:
questions.e: Cov(X, X) = Var(X).

questions.q: An eigenvalue between 0 and 1 means the eigenvector is:
questions.e: Direction is kept and the length shrinks.

questions.q: What defines an eigenvector of a matrix?
o: It becomes perpendicular to its original self
It keeps its direction under the transformation
It always has length exactly 1 afterwards
It is the largest column of the matrix
questions.e: It may be stretched, compressed or flipped along the same line.

questions.q: In PCA, the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is:
o: The original feature with the largest mean
The direction capturing the least variance
The direction capturing the most variance
questions.e: That is the first principal component.

questions.q: Eigenvalues [1.01, 1.6, 3.61, 2.5] sorted descending give which indices?
What does eigenvectors[:, sorted_indices] do?
o: Reorders the rows by sample score
Sorts the entries inside each column
Reorders the columns to match sorted eigenvalues
questions.e: Eigenvectors are stored as columns.

questions.q: PC1 for a student is computed as:
o: The covariance of the row with itself
The dot product of the row with the first eigenvector
The sum of the student's raw scores
The first eigenvalue times the row mean
questions.e: Z = X times eigenvector.

questions.q: What does PCA treat as information?
questions.e: High-variance directions are preserved.

questions.q: With eigenvalues 3.9566, 0.0338, 0.0079, 0.0016, what share does PC1 explain?
questions.e: 3.9566 divided by their sum of about 4.

questions.q: List the steps of PCA in order.
questions.m: Standardize the data, compute the covariance matrix, compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors, sort them in descending order, and project the data onto the top k eigenvectors.

questions.q: What do eigenvalues and eigenvectors each represent in PCA?
questions.m: Eigenvalues give the amount of variance carried by each principal component. Eigenvectors give the directions of those components in the original feature space.

questions.q: A standardized row is [1, 2] and the first eigenvector is [0.6, 0.8]. Compute PC1.
What does t-SNE mainly preserve?
questions.e: It keeps nearby points together.

questions.q: What does very low perplexity tend to produce?
questions.e: Too few neighbours are considered.

questions.q: What is the typical sweet spot for perplexity?
questions.e: From the slide.

questions.q: Which reading of a t-SNE plot can you trust?
questions.e: The other three are explicitly warned against.

questions.q: Which is true of t-SNE compared with PCA?
o: It is best used for model features
It is much faster on large data
It needs a refit for new points
questions.e: PCA can transform new points; t-SNE cannot.

questions.q: You need a 2-D input for a classifier used on new data tomorrow. Which method?
questions.e: PCA learns a reusable transformation.

questions.q: Running PCA before t-SNE can:
o: Give the axes a fixed meaning
Speed it up and reduce noise
Force clusters to be equal in size
questions.e: The slide marks this statement true.

questions.q: t-SNE adjusts point positions by minimizing:
questions.e: Slide 14 names it.

questions.q: Name three things you should not over-read in a t-SNE plot.
questions.m: Distance between clusters, cluster size and density, and the axes, which have no fixed meaning and can rotate or flip between runs.

questions.q: Compare PCA and t-SNE on type, what they preserve, and use.
questions.m: PCA is linear, preserves global variance and suits preprocessing. t-SNE is non-linear, preserves local neighbourhoods and suits visual exploration.

questions.q: For the rare disease example, P(disease | positive) is about:
Why is P(disease | positive) so low?
o: The disease rate rises after testing
False positives from healthy people outnumber true positives
questions.e: There are 9.99 false positives against 0.99 true positives.

questions.q: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter that:
o: Minimizes the size of the sample
Makes the observed data most probable
questions.e: It maximizes P(data | theta).

questions.q: What does Bayesian MAP estimation add compared with MLE?
o: A prior belief about the parameter
questions.e: The posterior combines likelihood and prior.

questions.q: The Law of Large Numbers says that as trials increase:
o: The sample average approaches the expected mean
The sample variance grows without limit
questions.e: Only the average converges.

questions.q: The Central Limit Theorem concerns the distribution of:
questions.e: Means become approximately normal.

questions.q: Which is a condition for the CLT on the slide?
questions.e: The population can be any shape.

questions.q: An attribute shared by every character in "Guess Who" carries:
questions.e: Common attributes tell you little.

questions.q: High entropy means:
questions.e: Entropy measures uncertainty.

questions.q: Disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity 90%, false positive rate 9%. Find P(disease | positive).
Explain the difference between the Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem.
questions.m: LLN says the sample mean converges to the true mean as the sample grows. CLT says the distribution of sample means is approximately normal for large samples, whatever the population shape.

questions.q: A sample mean is an example of a:
questions.e: It is calculated from sample data.

questions.q: "We are 95% confident the mean is between 50 and 60" is:
questions.e: It gives a range.

questions.q: The null hypothesis is:
o: The default assumption of no effect
The claim that a difference exists
The threshold for rejecting a claim
The probability of the observed result
questions.e: H1 is the claim being tested.

questions.q: The p-value is the probability of:
o: H0 being true given the data
H1 being true given the data
Observing the result if H0 is true
questions.e: It is conditional on H0.

questions.q: For two independent groups of 20 and 22, what is the df with equal variances?
With t = 2.27 and critical value 2.021 at alpha = 0.05, you should:
questions.e: 2.27 exceeds 2.021.

questions.q: Two classifiers are scored on the same 10 folds. Which test fits?
o: One-sample test on model A only
questions.e: Scores on the same fold are matched.

questions.q: For the paired test on 10 folds, the degrees of freedom are:
A medical test tells a healthy person they have a disease. This is:
questions.e: A false alarm.

questions.q: Which change directly reduces Type II errors?
questions.e: Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors.

questions.q: Define Type I and Type II errors with a medical example of each.
questions.m: Type I is rejecting a true H0, a false positive: a healthy person is told they are ill. Type II is failing to reject a false H0, a false negative: a real disease is missed.

questions.q: Fold differences have mean 0.03 and standard deviation 0.01 over n = 25 folds. Compute t and df.
Explain what a p-value of 0.03 means at alpha = 0.05.
questions.m: If H0 were true, there would be a 3% chance of a result at least this extreme. Since 0.03 is below 0.05, we reject H0.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of evaluating with one train/test split?
o: It cannot compute an accuracy for the model
The score depends on which rows land in the test set
It needs more data than cross-validation does
questions.e: Different random splits give noticeably different scores.

questions.q: Why is tuning a model on the test set a problem?
o: It removes the need for hyperparameters
Tuning cannot run on a held-out sample
It makes the training loss rise
The score then measures our own choices
questions.e: The slide says we are no longer measuring the future.

questions.q: In 5-fold cross-validation, how often is each fold the validation set?
questions.e: Each fold validates exactly once.

questions.q: What does the standard deviation of the k scores tell you?
o: The model's bias on the test set
Which fold has the most rows
How many fits grid search needs
questions.e: The mean estimates performance; the spread shows stability.

questions.q: Which is a hyperparameter?
o: The mean of the fold scores
A prediction on a validation row
A value set before training, such as C
questions.e: Weights are parameters, learned from data.

questions.q: A grid has 3 values of C and 4 of gamma, with 5 folds. How many fits?
questions.e: 3 x 4 = 12 combinations, times 5 folds.

questions.q: How does grid search choose the winner?
o: The first combination that trains without error
The combination with the lowest training loss
The combination with the best mean CV score
The combination with the most hyperparameters
questions.e: Each combination is scored with k-fold cross-validation.

questions.q: Describe the steps of k-fold cross-validation and what you report.
questions.m: Split the training data into k equal folds. Hold out one for validation, train on the other k-1, and repeat k times so each fold validates once. Report the mean of the k scores with their standard deviation.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter.
questions.m: Parameters, such as weights, are learned from the data. Hyperparameters are set by us before training, and grid search compares candidate values.
